{"schema":"voice-draft-source/4","kind":"draft","draft":"# The server was part of the appliance.

The server was part of the appliance. When a vendor closes the cloud service behind your connected home device, it hasn't merely stopped offering a bonus. It has reached into the appliance you bought and removed a piece of it – the piece that happened to live in somebody else's data center.

Consider what the shutdown can take. The camera may still contain a lens, sensor, radio, and processor, but it can't send alerts or show recordings in the app. The thermostat may still switch a relay, but schedules, remote controls, energy reports, and integrations can vanish. Your speaker may retain perfectly good microphones and amplifiers while losing the service that understood commands (or appeared to). What, exactly, still works?

Sometimes the answer is “a little.” A lightbulb may keep obeying its wall switch. A lock may still accept a physical key. But the routines you assembled, the automations tied to other devices, and the controls you use away from home can all depend on a remote computer. The plastic was delivered to your house; part of the machine remained behind the vendor's walls.

That arrangement changes the meaning of “buy.” You paid once, carried the object home, and reasonably treated it as yours. The vendor may answer that its terms allowed the service to change or disappear (terms drafted by the vendor, naturally). Sure, operating servers costs money, companies fail, and products age. But does that make a sale temporary whenever the seller designed the product to need continuing permission?

I don't think it does. A shutdown alters the original bargain because the vendor collected the purchase price for a working system, then retained a kill switch over essential functions. You bore the replacement cost; it controlled the dependency. I call that a rigged arcade machine – you bought the cabinet, paid for the controls, and discovered that the game board was rented from an operator who could unplug it whenever the tickets stopped paying.

Local operation changes who holds that plug. If commands, schedules, recordings, and automations run inside the home, the appliance can keep doing its ordinary job when the vendor's server closes. Your internet can fail without taking the light switch with it. The manufacturer can go bankrupt without bricking the lock. I don't mean every feature must avoid the network: remote access, off-site backup, and outside information may genuinely need one (weather forecasts are not generated by thermostats).

The protection comes from separating optional service from basic function. Local controls should work without an account. Devices should expose documented interfaces so another controller can operate them. Owners should be able to export settings and recordings in usable formats. Security updates matter too, of course, but “we need updates” isn't an argument for “we get permanent control.” We can have signed updates, secure local networks, and revocable remote access without making every appliance a hostage.

I would also treat shutdown plans as part of the product, not an act of corporate grace. Before you buy, ask which functions survive without the vendor's app and servers. Ask whether the device uses an open protocol, whether another hub can control it, and whether your data can be exported. If the answers are vague, you're being asked to finance a machine whose expiration date is hidden.

This isn't merely about rescuing old gadgets. It's about restoring a plain rule: sellers shouldn't keep technical power to repossess function after a sale. We need products designed so that the end of a cloud service becomes an inconvenience, not an eviction. Otherwise “connected appliance” is bullshit bookkeeping – the server remains part of the appliance, while the owner is told it never belonged to them.","omitted":[],"refused":""}
